newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: No more wool stockpile sale changes - Canberra.
newsitem.headline: No more wool stockpile sale changes - Canberra.

text.p: Australian Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said on Wednesday there would be no further changes to the new wool stockpile selling methods.
Anderson said he was responding to speculation that he would change wool stockpile legislation he introduced into parliament in late October.

"I introduced legislation on October 30 to implement the outcome of the wool roundtable, which is a most important piece of legislation because it symbolises unity in the wool industry and reflects an outcome which I have worked very hard to achieve," he said in a statement. "This outcome will stand."
The legislation relates to changes agreed on at a wool industry roundtable meeting in August on the release of stockpile wool for sale to the trade.
The changes involved introduction of a minimum quarterly release requirement of 135,000 bales from January 1, 1997, and a minimum quarterly release of 90,000 bales from July 1, 1997.
A maximum quarterly release of 350,000 bales will apply from January 1, 1997.
The end date for completion of stockpile sales and deliveries is December 31, 2000.
Present arrangements require quarterly sales of 182,000 to 192,000 bales which the industry said was too inflexible in relation to market trends.
Anderson said he was most concerned about the misinterpretation of the government's commitment to the roundtable outcome.
"I have decided that there is no basis for a review and as far as I am concerned the issue is closed," he said.
A spokesman for Anderson later said the lower house of parliament, the House of Representatives, was currently considering the legislation.
The bill was expected to be debated in the upper house Senate in the next few weeks, he said.
Wool Council of Australia president Rod Thirkell-Johnston welcomed Anderson's statement, saying the decision met the council's view that the stockpile debate was complete.
"I endorse the Minister's role in securing the roundtable stockpile changes and his commitment to industry deregulation," Thirkell-Johnston said in a statement.
The stockpile now stands just above two million bales, against its peak of 4.7 million bales.
